questions.q: Read six numbers into a grid of two rows of three.

teach.say: A two-dimensional list is a list whose items are themselves lists. Build each row as its own list, then append that row to the grid.

brief: Read six whole numbers, one on each line.
The first three are row 0 and the last three are row 1.
Print the grid itself, for example: [[9, 4, 1], [7, 0, 2]]
questions.starter: # Two rows of three, then print the grid

tests.why: Two sets of square brackets inside one. If you got [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] you made one flat list instead of a list of lists.
The numbers fill the first row before the second - reading them down the columns would give [[9, 7, 5], [8, 6, 4]].
Build a fresh inner list for each row - reusing the same one leaves both rows pointing at the same three numbers.

questions.fb: Make an empty row list, append three numbers to it, then append that row to the grid - and start a new row list for the next row.

questions.q: Print the number of rows, the row length, then one row.
brief: Read six names into a grid of three rows of two.
Then read one whole number: a row number counting from 0.
Print how many rows there are, how many names are in a row, then that row.
questions.starter: # Three rows of two names, then report on one row

tests.why: len(grid) counts the rows and len(grid[0]) counts the names in one row - here that is 3 and 2, so mixing them up shows at once.
Row 1 is the second row. Printing Ada and Bram means you counted the rows from 1.
Three rows means 2 is the last row number - adding 1 would run off the end of the grid.
Different names, so a row typed in by hand will fail here. Printing grid[r] gives the brackets and quotes for you.

questions.fb: A grid is a list of lists, so len(grid) is the number of rows and len(grid[r]) is the number of items in one row.

questions.q: Print the value stored at a typed row and column.

teach.say: Two sets of brackets: the first picks a row out of the grid, the second picks an item out of that row.

brief: Read nine whole numbers into a grid of three rows of three.
Then read a row number and a column number, both counting from 0.
Print the value stored there, and nothing else.
questions.starter: # Three rows of three, then one value out of it

tests.why: Row 0, column 0 is the very first value. Printing 8 means you took grid[1][1], so both numbers were counted from 1.
The row comes first and the column second - grid[2][1] would give 3 instead.
This is the test above with the two numbers swapped, so it fails any program that reads the column first.
Three rows of three means the last value is at [2][2] - [3][3] is past the end of the grid.
A different grid, so a value typed in by hand will fail here.

questions.fb: grid[r] is a whole row and grid[r][c] is one item of that row, so the row always comes first.

questions.q: Print one whole row and one whole column of the grid.
brief: Read nine whole numbers into a grid of three rows of three.
Then read a row number and a column number, both counting from 0.
Print that row on one line, then that column, with single spaces between the values.
questions.starter: # One row across, one column down

tests.why: The row runs across and the column runs down, so they share only the first value. Two identical lines means you printed the row twice.
Row 2 and column 2 are the last of each. Counting from 1 would crash or give the wrong line here.
A whole row is just grid[r], but a column has to be gathered by taking grid[i][c] from every row in turn.

questions.fb: A row is one item of the grid; a column is not stored anywhere, so you collect it one row at a time.

questions.q: Print six numbers back as two tidy rows of three.

teach.say: A loop over a grid hands you one row at a time, and a loop inside it walks along that row.

brief: Read six whole numbers into a grid of two rows of three.
Print each row on its own line, with single spaces between the values.
Print no square brackets and no commas.
questions.starter: # Two rows in, two tidy lines out

tests.why: Two lines of three. Printing the grid itself would give the brackets and commas the brief rules out.
The rows stay separate even when the values repeat - a single print inside both loops would give six lines instead of two.
Build the whole line first and print it once, or use print(v, end=' ') and then an empty print at the end of each row.

questions.fb: The outer loop is the rows and the inner loop is the values in one row - the line break belongs to the outer loop.

questions.q: Print the row, column and value of every cell.
brief: Read nine whole numbers into a grid of three rows of three.
Print each cell's row, column and value, separated by single spaces.
One line per cell, all of row 0 first, counting from 0.
questions.starter: # Visit every cell and say where it is

tests.why: The first line must be 0 0 1. If it says 1 1 1 you started both counts at 1 instead of 0.
With every value the same, only the positions change - this shows plainly that they run 0 to 2 in both directions.
Nine lines in total. Six or three means one of the loops is not running the full three times, or the print is in the wrong loop.

questions.fb: The outer loop counts rows and the inner loop counts columns, so the inner one finishes once for every single step of the outer one.

questions.q: Print the total of one row of the grid.

teach.say: grid[r] is one whole row, and a row is an ordinary list, so you can total it the way you would total any list.

brief: Read twelve whole numbers into a grid of three rows of four.
Then read one whole number: a row number counting from 0.
Print the total of that row, and nothing else.
questions.starter: # Three rows of four, then the total of one row

tests.why: Row 0 is 2, 5, 3, 1 which comes to 11. An answer of 15 is row 1, which means you counted the rows from 1.
Total the four values in one row, not the first value of every row - that would give 6 whichever row was asked for.
Zeros add nothing but the loop still has to visit them, so 0, 0, 9, 3 comes to 12.
A row of zeros still has a total, and it still has to be printed. Three rows means 2 is the last row number.

questions.fb: merits[r] is a single row and behaves like any other list, so a running total over it works exactly as it always did.

questions.q: Print the total of each row, then of the whole grid.
brief: Read twelve whole numbers into a grid of three rows of four.
Print the total of each row, one on each line, starting with row 0.
Then print the total of the whole grid.
questions.starter: # A total for each row, then one for everything

tests.why: Three row totals and then the grand total, so four lines in all - forgetting the last line loses a mark even if the rows are right.
A row of zeros still prints its total of 0 - it must not be skipped.
If every row total is the same as the grand total you forgot to reset the row total back to 0 at the start of each row.

questions.fb: Set the row total to 0 inside the outer loop, and keep a separate grand total outside it that never gets reset.

questions.q: Print the total of one column of the grid.

teach.say: A column is not stored anywhere, so you gather it one row at a time: the column number stays still while the row number changes.

brief: Read twelve whole numbers into a grid of four rows of three.
Then read one whole number: a column number counting from 0.
Print the total of that column, and nothing else.
questions.starter: # Four rows of three, then the total of one column

tests.why: Column 0 is 3, 5, 0, 9 which comes to 17. An answer of 12 means you totalled row 0 instead.
Gather the column with grid[r][c] from every row - the column number stays the same while the row number changes.
Three columns means 2 is the last one - counting from 1 would ask for column 3 and crash.
Every value in column 1 is 0, so the total is 0. A 4 here means you totalled column 0 whatever was asked for.

questions.fb: Loop over the rows with range(len(grid)) and hold the column number still - that is the one difference from totalling a row.

questions.q: Print the total of each column, then of the whole grid.
brief: Read twelve whole numbers into a grid of four rows of three.
Print the total of each column, one on each line, starting with column 0.
Then print the total of the whole grid.
questions.starter: # A total for each column, then one for everything

tests.why: Three column totals then the grand total. Getting 6, 15, 24, 33 means you totalled the rows instead of the columns.
Only column 0 has anything in it - the other two still print a total of 0 rather than being skipped.
Here it is the last column that holds everything, so a loop that stops one column short would print 0, 0 and then the wrong grand total.

questions.fb: For column totals the outer loop counts columns and the inner loop counts rows - the opposite way round to row totals.

questions.q: Find where a name sits, and how many share its row.

teach.say: Two loops over range(len(...)) visit every cell of a grid in turn, row by row.

brief: Read nine names into three rows of three. A free seat holds the word empty.
Then read a name. If it is nowhere in the grid, print only: not seated
Otherwise print its row and column, then how many seats in that row are not empty.
questions.starter: # Search the grid for the name, then count that row

tests.why: Nia is in the top left, which is row 0 column 0. Printing 1 1 means you counted rows and columns from 1.
Row first, then column. Printing 2 1 means the two were the wrong way round.
Yves is the very last seat, so a search that stops before the end of the last row never finds it. Nobody in row 2 is empty, so the count is 3.
Row 0 has one empty seat, so only two of its three seats count - the word empty must be skipped, not counted.
A name that is nowhere in the grid prints that one line and nothing else, so the row and column must only be printed once the name has been found.

questions.fb: Two loops to search every cell, a remembered row and column that start at something impossible like -1, then a separate loop over the found row to count the seats.
